attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his own post, said in his own voice.

semantics.note: The checkable core is a cumulative $1T 'burned' on generative AI. It sits inside a rhetorical sentence. The 'most-wasteful' ranking has no measure and can't be scored, which the contract rightly sets aside.

contract.note: Reading 'burned' as money spent is an ordinary reading in a post about capex. Still, 'burned' could also mean losses, and the start date, scope and allocation rules all come from the evaluator. The result depends on those choices.

evidence.note: One year (2025) of private investment received, $170.9B. That is funding, not cumulative realized spending, so it can't settle the $1T total.
News report of Gartner's April 2025 forecast for 2025 spending, which includes devices. It is a forecast, not realized cumulative spending, and the scope differs.

reviews.rationale: Nothing in the packet gives a reconciled cumulative total of realized generative-AI spending through May 19, 2026. The two items measure one year of funding and a forecast, so they neither confirm nor refute $1T. The wastefulness ranking can't be scored.

attribution.note: Zitron's own statement in his own post.

semantics.note: Keeps the universal 'every' and the hedged 'appears' in the second clause. It is an unqualified present-tense observation.

contract.note: Reading 'every' literally follows the speaker's own firm word. Choosing calendar 2025, net loss as the measure, and a $2M floor are evaluator choices, so the result depends on that interpretation.

evidence.note: Gamma's CEO says the company reached $100M ARR 'profitably'. This is the company's own claim, the profit measure and period are unstated, and ARR is not full-year net income. It is a strong lead but doesn't meet the contradiction condition.

reviews.rationale: Proving the universal claim would need accounts for the whole startup population, and the packet has none. The one counterexample, Gamma, rests on the company's own profitability claim with no full-year 2025 net income or accounting basis. It casts serious doubt on 'every' but does not meet the contract's contradiction test.

attribution.note: Zitron's own statement in his own post.

semantics.note: In context, 'them' means Microsoft, Meta, Amazon and Google. 'Will talk' describes how they disclose now, not a forecast. The surrounding text sets run rates aside.

contract.note: Requiring a realized AI revenue amount, and excluding run rates and growth percentages, matches the speaker's own dismissal of run rates. Whether 'talk about' covers growth figures or testimony about one customer is an interpretive choice that affects the result.

evidence.note: Microsoft gives only an annualized run rate, which fits the claim. But this doesn't show that no other disclosure exists.
AWS segment revenue covers more than AI, so it is not an AI revenue amount.
Google reports revenue growth for its generative-AI products but no dollar amount. Under a broad reading of 'talk about', this would count against the claim.
Meta gives segment totals and mentions AI glasses but no company-wide AI revenue amount.
Court testimony disclosed $9.5B of revenue from the OpenAI partnership through March 2025. It covers one partnership and a different period, so it is outside the target quarter.

reviews.rationale: The main Q1 2026 disclosures from all four companies are consistent with the claim: each gives only run rates, growth figures or segment totals. But proving a universal negative needs complete coverage of their disclosures. Some primary pages couldn't be read, and Google's growth figure and Microsoft's testimony complicate a broader reading, so the packet does not settle the claim.

attribution.note: Zitron's own arithmetic claim in his own post.

semantics.note: The $45B figure and zero opex are stipulated inputs. The checkable part is a comparison with each named company's reported capex for 2023 and 2024.

contract.note: The speaker's 'Microsoft, Google, Meta, or Amazon' plus 'a single year' points to each company separately, not a combined total. Testing every company-year against $45B is the ordinary reading.

evidence.note: Meta's 2023 annual report puts capex at $28.10B, well under $45B. Meta and 2023 are both named in the claim.

reviews.rationale: Meta reported $28.10B of capex for 2023, finance-lease principal included. That is $16.9B less than $45B, so the stipulated revenue would have covered that named company-year. The contract says one such case disproves the claim.
